“Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu navakammaṃ gahetvā pariyosite vibbhamati…pe… kālaṅkaroti, sāmaṇero paṭijānāti, sikkhaṃ paccakkhātako paṭijānāti, antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpannako paṭijānāti – saṅgho sāmī.

“Here, monks, if a monk, having undertaken new work, disrobes after it is finished… or dies, or declares himself a novice, or declares himself one who has renounced the training, or declares himself one who has committed an ultimate offense—the Sangha is the owner.

“Idha [V 0.0306] pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu navakammaṃ gahetvā pariyosite ummattako paṭijānāti, khittacitto paṭijānāti, vedanāṭṭo paṭijānāti, āpattiyā adassane ukkhittako paṭijānāti, āpattiyā appaṭikamme ukkhittako paṭijānāti, pāpikāya diṭṭhiyā appaṭinissagge [P 2.0174] ukkhittako paṭijānāti – tassevetaṃ.

“Here, monks, if a monk, having undertaken new work, declares himself to be insane after it is finished, or declares himself to be of distracted mind, or declares himself to be afflicted by pain, or declares himself to be one suspended for not seeing an offense, or declares himself to be one suspended for not making amends for an offense, or declares himself to be one suspended for not relinquishing a wicked view—it belongs to that very monk.

“Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu navakammaṃ gahetvā pariyosite paṇḍako paṭijānāti, theyyasaṃvāsako paṭijānāti, titthiyapakkantako paṭijānāti, tiracchānagato paṭijānāti, mātughātako paṭijānāti, pitughātako paṭijānāti, arahantaghātako paṭijānāti, bhikkhunīdūsako paṭijānāti, saṅghabhedako paṭijānāti, lohituppādako paṭijānāti, ubhatobyañjanako paṭijānāti – saṅgho sāmī”ti.

“Here, monks, if a monk, having undertaken new work, declares himself to be a paṇḍaka after it is finished, or declares himself to be one in communion by theft, or declares himself to be one who has gone over to another sect, or declares himself to be an animal, or declares himself to be a matricide, or declares himself to be a patricide, or declares himself to be a killer of an Arahant, or declares himself to be a violator of a bhikkhunī, or declares himself to be a schismatic, or declares himself to be one who has shed the Buddha's blood, or declares himself to be an ubhatobyañjanaka—the Sangha is the owner.”

Aññatraparibhogapaṭikkhepādi

Prohibition of Use Elsewhere, etc.

324. pārā. 157 Tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū aññatarassa upāsakassa vihāraparibhogaṃ senāsanaṃ aññatra paribhuñjanti. Atha kho so upāsako ujjhāyati khiyyati vipāceti – “kathañhi nāma bhadantā aññatra [T 2.0143] paribhogaṃ aññatra paribhuñjissantī”ti! Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Na, bhikkhave, aññatra paribhogo aññatra paribhuñjitabbo. Yo paribhuñjeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti.

324. At that time, monks were using the lodging and furnishings, which were for the use of a monastery of a certain lay follower, in another place. Then that lay follower complained, criticized, and disparaged, saying: 'How indeed can the venerable sirs use furnishings meant for one place in another place?' They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, furnishings for one place should not be used in another place. Whoever should use them commits an offense of wrong conduct.'

pārā. 157 Tena [M 0.0328] kho pana samayena bhikkhū uposathaggampi sannisajjampi harituṃ kukkuccāyantā chamāya nisīdanti. Gattānipi cīvarānipi paṃsukitāni honti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tāvakālikaṃ haritu”nti.

At that time monks, being scrupulous, hesitated to carry things to the Uposatha hall and the assembly place, and sat on the ground. Their bodies and also their robes became dusty. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, I allow you to carry them for a temporary period.'

Tena kho pana samayena saṅghassa mahāvihāro undriyati. Bhikkhū kukkuccāyantā senāsanaṃ nātiharanti nābhiharanti (ka.). Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, guttatthāya haritu”nti.

At that time the great monastery of the Sangha was collapsing. Monks, being scrupulous, did not move the lodgings. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, I allow you to move them for the sake of safekeeping.'

Tena kho pana samayena saṅghassa senāsanaparikkhāriko mahaggho kambalo uppanno hoti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, phātikammatthāya parivattetu”nti.

At that time, a very valuable blanket, a requisite for the lodging, had arisen for the Saṅgha. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, I allow it to be exchanged for the sake of making it profitable.'

Tena [V 0.0307] kho pana samayena saṅghassa senāsanaparikkhārikaṃ mahagghaṃ dussaṃ uppannaṃ hoti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, phātikammatthāya parivattetu”nti.

At that time, a valuable cloth, a requisite for the lodging, had arisen for the Saṅgha. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, I allow it to be exchanged for the sake of making it profitable.'

Tena kho pana samayena saṅghassa acchacammaṃ uppannaṃ hoti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pādapuñchaniṃ kātu”nti.

At that time, a bear's hide had arisen for the Saṅgha. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, I allow the making of a foot-wiper.'

Tena kho pana samayena saṅghassa cakkalikaṃ uppannaṃ hoti[T 2.0144]. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pādapuñchaniṃ kātu”nti.

At that time, a circular mat had arisen for the Saṅgha. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, I allow the making of a foot-wiper.'

Tena kho pana samayena saṅghassa coḷakaṃ uppannaṃ hoti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pādapuñchaniṃ kātu”nti.

At that time, a piece of cloth had arisen for the Saṅgha. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, I allow the making of a foot-wiper.'

Tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū adhotehi pādehi senāsanaṃ akkamanti. Senāsanaṃ dussati. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Na, bhikkhave, adhotehi pādehi senāsanaṃ akkamitabbaṃ. Yo akkameyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti.

At that time, monks were stepping on the lodging with unwashed feet. The lodging was damaged. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, the lodging is not to be stepped on with unwashed feet. Whoever should step on it, commits an offense of wrong conduct.'

Tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū allehi pādehi senāsanaṃ akkamanti. Senāsanaṃ dussati. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ[P 2.0175]. “Na, bhikkhave, allehi pādehi senāsanaṃ akkamitabbaṃ. Yo akkameyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti.

At that time, monks were stepping on the lodging with wet feet. The lodging was damaged. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, the lodging is not to be stepped on with wet feet. Whoever should step on it, commits an offense of wrong conduct.'

Tena [M 0.0329] kho pana samayena bhikkhū saupāhanā senāsanaṃ akkamanti. Senāsanaṃ dussati. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Na, bhikkhave, saupāhanena senāsanaṃ akkamitabbaṃ. Yo akkameyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti.

At that time, monks wearing footwear were stepping on the lodging. The lodging was damaged. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, the lodging is not to be stepped on by one wearing footwear. Whoever should step on it, commits an offense of wrong conduct.'

Tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū parikammakatāya bhūmiyā niṭṭhubhanti. Vaṇṇo dussati. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Na[T 2.0145], bhikkhave, parikammakatāya bhūmiyā niṭṭhubhitabbaṃ. Yo niṭṭhubheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, kheḷamallaka”nti.

At that time monks were spitting on a prepared floor. The appearance was spoiled. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “Monks, a prepared floor should not be spat upon. Whoever spits upon it, commits an offense of wrong conduct. I allow, monks, a spittoon.”

Tena kho pana samayena mañcapādāpi pīṭhapādāpi parikammakataṃ bhūmiṃ vilikhanti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, coḷakena paliveṭhetu”nti.

At that time, the legs of couches and benches scratched the prepared floor. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, monks, to wrap them with a piece of cloth.”

Tena [V 0.0308] kho pana samayena bhikkhū parikammakataṃ bhittiṃ apassenti. Vaṇṇo dussati. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Na, bhikkhave, parikammakatā bhitti apassetabbā. Yo apasseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, apassenaphalaka”nti. Apassenaphalakaṃ heṭṭhato bhūmiṃ vilikhati, uparito bhittiñca. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, heṭṭhato ca uparito ca coḷakena paliveṭhetu”nti.

At that time the monks were leaning against a prepared wall. The surface was spoiled. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “Monks, a prepared wall should not be leaned against. Whoever leans against it, commits an offense of wrong conduct. I allow, monks, a backrest board.” The backrest board scratched the ground below and the wall above. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, monks, to wrap it with a piece of cloth both below and above.”

Tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū dhotapādakā nipajjituṃ kukkuccāyanti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, paccattharitvā nipajjitu”nti.

At that time monks, having washed their feet, were scrupulous about lying down. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow, monks, to lie down after spreading a covering.”

Saṅghabhattādianujānanaṃ

Allowance for Community Meals, etc.

325. Atha kho bhagavā āḷaviyaṃ yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā yena rājagahaṃ tena cārikaṃ pakkāmi. Anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena rājagahaṃ tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Tena [T 2.0146] kho pana samayena rājagahaṃ dubbhikkhaṃ hoti. Manussā na sakkonti saṅghabhattaṃ kātuṃ; icchanti uddesabhattaṃ nimantanaṃ salākabhattaṃ pakkhikaṃ uposathikaṃ pāṭipadikaṃ kātuṃ. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, saṅghabhattaṃ uddesabhattaṃ nimantanaṃ salākabhattaṃ pakkhikaṃ uposathikaṃ pāṭipadika”nti.

325. Then the Blessed One, having stayed in Āḷavī as long as he pleased, set out on a journey to Rājagaha. Wandering on tour in stages, he arrived at Rājagaha. There the Blessed One stayed in Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. At that time, there was a famine in Rājagaha. People were unable to prepare a meal for the Saṅgha; they wished to prepare a meal designated from the Saṅgha, an invitation meal, a meal distributed by ticket, a fortnightly meal, an Uposatha day meal, and a meal on the day after Uposatha. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “Monks, I allow a meal for the Saṅgha, a meal designated from the Saṅgha, an invitation meal, a meal distributed by ticket, a fortnightly meal, an Uposatha day meal, and a meal on the day after Uposatha.”

Bhattuddesakasammuti

The Appointment of a Meal-Assigner

326. Tena [M 0.0330] kho pana samayena chabbaggiyā bhikkhū attano varabhattāni gahetvā lāmakāni bhattāni bhikkhūnaṃ denti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgataṃ bhikkhuṃ bhattuddesakaṃ [P 2.0176] sammannituṃ – yo na chandāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na dosāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na mohāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na bhayāgatiṃ gaccheyya, uddiṭṭhānuddiṭṭhañca jāneyya. Evañca pana, bhikkhave, sammannitabbo. Paṭhamaṃ bhikkhu yācitabbo, yācitvā byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena saṅgho ñāpetabbo –

326. At that time, the monks of the group of six would take the excellent meals for themselves and give the inferior meals to the other monks. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “Monks, I allow a monk endowed with five factors to be appointed as a meal-assigner: one who would not go the wrong way through desire, would not go the wrong way through hatred, would not go the wrong way through delusion, would not go the wrong way through fear, and who would know what has been assigned and what has not been assigned. And, monks, he is to be appointed in this way. First, a monk should be requested; having requested, the Saṅgha should be informed by a clever and capable monk:

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhattuddesakaṃ sammanneyya. Esā ñatti.

“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. If the time is right for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named so-and-so as a meal-assigner. This is the motion.

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho. Saṅgho itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhattuddesakaṃ sammannati. Yassāyasmato [V 0.0309] khamati itthannāmassa bhikkhuno bhattuddesakassa sammuti, so tuṇhassa; yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya.

“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. The Saṅgha appoints the monk named so-and-so as a meal-assigner. To whichever venerable one the appointment of the monk named so-and-so as a meal-assigner is agreeable, he should be silent; to whomever it is not agreeable, he should speak.

“Sammato saṅghena itthannāmo bhikkhu bhattuddesako. Khamati [T 2.0147] saṅghassa, tasmā tuṇhī, evametaṃ dhārayāmī”ti.

“The monk named so-and-so has been appointed by the Saṅgha as a meal-assigner. It is agreeable to the Saṅgha, therefore there is silence. Thus I hold it.”

Atha kho bhattuddesakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – “kathaṃ nu kho bhattaṃ uddisitabba”nti? Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, salākāya vā paṭṭikāya vā paṭikāya vā (syā.) upanibandhitvā opuñjitvā bhattaṃ uddisitu”nti.

Then this thought arose in the monks who were meal-designators: 'How, indeed, should the meal be designated?' They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, I allow the meal to be designated by means of a bamboo slip or a tablet, having written on them and mixed them up.'

Senāsanapaññāpakādisammuti

Appointment of the Arranger of Lodgings and Others

327. Tena kho pana samayena saṅghassa senāsanapaññāpako na hoti…pe… bhaṇḍāgāriko na hoti…pe… cīvarappaṭiggāhako na hoti…pe… cīvarabhājako na hoti…pe… yāgubhājako na hoti…pe… phalabhājako na hoti…pe… khajjakabhājako na hoti. Khajjakaṃ abhājiyamānaṃ nassati. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgataṃ bhikkhuṃ khajjakabhājakaṃ sammannituṃ – yo na chandāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na dosāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na mohāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na bhayāgatiṃ gaccheyya[M 0.0331], bhājitābhājitañca jāneyya. Evañca pana, bhikkhave, sammannitabbo. Paṭhamaṃ bhikkhu yācitabbo, yācitvā byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena saṅgho ñāpetabbo –

327. At that time the Saṅgha had no arranger of lodgings... no storekeeper... no robe-receiver... no robe-distributor... no gruel-distributor... no fruit-distributor... no distributor of hard food. The hard food, not being distributed, was being wasted. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, I allow a monk endowed with five factors to be appointed as a distributor of hard food: one who would not go the wrong way through desire, would not go the wrong way through hatred, would not go the wrong way through delusion, would not go the wrong way through fear, and who would know what has been distributed and what has not. And, monks, he should be appointed thus: First, a monk should be requested. Having made the request, an experienced and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ khajjakabhājakaṃ sammanneyya. Esā ñatti.

'Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named so-and-so as the distributor of hard food. This is the motion.'

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho. Saṅgho itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ khajjakabhājakaṃ sammannati[T 2.0148]. Yassāyasmato khamati itthannāmassa bhikkhuno khajjakabhājakassa sammuti, so tuṇhassa; yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya.

'Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. The Saṅgha appoints the monk named so-and-so as the distributor of hard food. Whichever venerable one approves of the appointment of the monk named so-and-so as the distributor of hard food, he should remain silent; whomever does not approve, he should speak.'

“Sammato saṅghena itthannāmo bhikkhu khajjakabhājako. Khamati saṅghassa, tasmā tuṇhī, evametaṃ dhārayāmī”ti.

'The monk named so-and-so has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the distributor of hard food. It is approved by the Saṅgha, therefore there is silence. Thus I take it.'

Appamattakavissajjakasammuti

Appointment of the Distributor of Minor Items

328. Tena [V 0.0310] kho pana samayena saṅghassa bhaṇḍāgāre appamattako parikkhāro uppanno ussanno (syā.) hoti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgataṃ [P 2.0177] bhikkhuṃ appamattakavissajjakaṃ sammannituṃ – yo na chandāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na dosāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na mohāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na bhayāgatiṃ gaccheyya, vissajjitāvissajjitañca jāneyya. Evañca pana, bhikkhave, sammannitabbo. Paṭhamaṃ bhikkhu yācitabbo, yācitvā byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena saṅgho ñāpetabbo –

328. Now at that time, a small amount of requisites had arisen in the Saṅgha’s storeroom. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, I allow a monk endowed with five factors to be appointed as a distributor of minor items: one who would not go the wrong way through desire, would not go the wrong way through hatred, would not go the wrong way through delusion, would not go the wrong way through fear, and who would know what has been given away and what has not. And, monks, he should be appointed thus: First, a monk should be requested. Having made the request, an experienced and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ appamattakavissajjakaṃ sammanneyya. Esā ñatti.

'Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named so-and-so as the distributor of minor items. This is the motion.'

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho. Saṅgho itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ appamattakavissajjakaṃ sammannati. Yassāyasmato khamati itthannāmassa bhikkhuno appamattakavissajjakassa sammuti, so tuṇhassa; yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya.

'Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. The Saṅgha appoints the monk named so-and-so as the distributor of minor items. Whichever venerable one approves of the appointment of the monk named so-and-so as the distributor of minor items, he should remain silent; whomever does not approve, he should speak.'

“Sammato saṅghena itthannāmo bhikkhu appamattakavissajjako. Khamati saṅghassa, tasmā tuṇhī[T 2.0149], evametaṃ dhārayāmī”ti.

'The monk named so-and-so has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the distributor of minor items. It is approved by the Saṅgha, therefore there is silence. Thus I take it.'

Tena [M 0.0332] appamattakavissajjakena bhikkhunā ekā ekekā (sī.) sūci dātabbā, satthakaṃ dātabbaṃ, upāhanā dātabbā, kāyabandhanaṃ dātabbaṃ, aṃsabandhako dātabbo, parissāvanaṃ dātabbaṃ, dhammakaraṇo dātabbo, kusi dātabbā, aḍḍhakusi dātabbā, maṇḍalaṃ dātabbaṃ, aḍḍhamaṇḍalaṃ dātabbaṃ, anuvāto dātabbo, paribhaṇḍaṃ dātabbaṃ. Sace hoti saṅghassa sappi vā telaṃ vā madhu vā phāṇitaṃ vā, sakiṃ paṭisāyituṃ dātabbaṃ. Sace punapi attho hoti, punapi dātabbaṃ.

By that monk, the distributor of minor items, a needle should be given, a small knife should be given, sandals should be given, a waistband should be given, a shoulder-strap should be given, a water-strainer should be given, a dhammakaraṇa should be given, a large shuttle should be given, a small shuttle should be given, a circular frame should be given, a semi-circular frame should be given, a lengthwise border should be given, and a crosswise border should be given. If there is for the Saṅgha ghee, or oil, or honey, or molasses, it should be given to be consumed once. If there is need again, it should be given again.

Sāṭiyaggāhāpakādisammuti

Appointment of the Distributor of Rain-Cloths and Others

329. Tena kho pana samayena saṅghassa sāṭiyaggāhāpako na hoti…pe… pattaggāhāpako na hoti…pe… ārāmikapesako na hoti…pe… sāmaṇerapesako na hoti. Sāmaṇerā apesiyamānā kammaṃ na karonti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahaṅgehi samannāgataṃ bhikkhuṃ sāmaṇerapesakaṃ sammannituṃ – yo na chandāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na dosāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na mohāgatiṃ gaccheyya, na bhayāgatiṃ gaccheyya, pesitāpesitañca [V 0.0311] jāneyya. Evañca pana, bhikkhave, sammannitabbo. Paṭhamaṃ bhikkhu yācitabbo, yācitvā byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena saṅgho ñāpetabbo –

329. Now at that time, the Saṅgha had no distributor of rain-cloths... no distributor of bowls... no one who sends monastery attendants... no one who sends novices. The novices, not being sent on errands, did not do their work. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. 'Monks, I allow a monk endowed with five factors to be appointed as one who sends novices: one who would not go the wrong way through desire, would not go the wrong way through hatred, would not go the wrong way through delusion, would not go the wrong way through fear, and who would know who has been sent and who has not. And, monks, he should be appointed thus: First, a monk should be requested. Having made the request, an experienced and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho [T 2.0150] itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ sāmaṇerapesakaṃ sammanneyya. Esā ñatti.

'Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named so-and-so as one who sends novices. This is the motion.'

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho. Saṅgho itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ sāmaṇerapesakaṃ sammannati. Yassāyasmato khamati itthannāmassa bhikkhuno sāmaṇerapesakassa sammuti, so tuṇhassa; yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya.

'Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me. The Saṅgha appoints the monk named so-and-so as one who sends novices. Whichever venerable one approves of the appointment of the monk named so-and-so as one who sends novices, he should remain silent; whomever does not approve, he should speak.'

“Sammato saṅghena itthannāmo bhikkhu sāmaṇerapesako. Khamati saṅghassa, tasmā tuṇhī, evametaṃ dhārayāmī”ti.

'The monk named so-and-so has been appointed by the Saṅgha as one who sends novices. It is approved by the Saṅgha, therefore there is silence. Thus I take it.'

Tatiyabhāṇavāro niṭṭhito.

The third recitation section is concluded.

Senāsanakkhandhako chaṭṭho.

The sixth chapter on lodgings is concluded.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of it:

Vihāraṃ [M 0.0333] buddhaseṭṭhena, apaññattaṃ tadā ahu;

Tahaṃ tahaṃ nikkhamanti, vāsā te jinasāvakā.

A dwelling had not yet been laid down by the Supreme Buddha at that time; those disciples of the Conqueror departed from their dwellings here and there.

Seṭṭhī gahapati disvā, bhikkhūnaṃ idamabravi;

Kārāpeyyaṃ vaseyyātha, paṭipucchiṃsu nāyakaṃ.

The merchant householder, having seen the monks, said this: 'I would have dwellings made; would you dwell in them?' They in turn asked the Leader.

Vihāraṃ aḍḍhayogañca, pāsādaṃ hammiyaṃ guhaṃ;

Pañcaleṇaṃ anuññāsi, vihāre seṭṭhi kārayi.

A gabled monastery, a half-gabled building, a long-storied building, a flat-roofed storied building, and a cave—these five kinds of lodging He allowed. The great merchant had dwellings made.

Jano vihāraṃ kāreti, akavāṭaṃ asaṃvutaṃ;

Kavāṭaṃ piṭṭhasaṅghāṭaṃ, udukkhalañca uttari.

People had a dwelling made, without a door-leaf, unenclosed. A door-leaf, a door-post, a lower pivot-socket, and an upper pivot-socket.

Āviñchanacchiddaṃ [T 2.0151][V 0.0312] rajjuṃ, vaṭṭiñca kapisīsakaṃ;

Sūcighaṭitāḷacchiddaṃ[P 2.0178], lohakaṭṭhavisāṇakaṃ.

A hole for pulling, a rope, a bolt, and a monkey's head bolt-knob; a keyhole, and a key made of metal, wood, or horn.

Yantakaṃ sūcikañceva, chadanaṃ ullittāvalittaṃ;

Vedijālasalākañca, cakkali santharena ca.

A mechanism, and a small bolt; a roof, plastering inside and out; a railing, a latticework window and a window with slats, a circular foot-wiper, and a grass mat.

Miḍḍhi bidalamañcañca, sosānikamasārako;

Bundikuḷirapādañca, āhaccāsandi uccake.

Plastering with clay, and a couch woven with rattan; a couch from a charnel ground with legs fitted into the frame; a chair made by joining the beam and crossbar, a chair with curved legs, a chair with legs fitted into the seat-frame, a rectangular chair, and a high one.

Sattaṅgo ca bhaddapīṭhaṃ, pīṭhakeḷakapādakaṃ;

Āmalāphalakā kocchā, palālapīṭhameva ca.

A chair with seven parts, and a chair woven with rattan; a chair made of coarse cloth, a chair with goat-like legs; a floor-covering with many legs polished like an āmalaka fruit, a plank floor-covering, a mat, and also a straw chair.

Uccāhipaṭipādakā, aṭṭhaṅguli ca pādakā;

Suttaṃ aṭṭhapadaṃ coḷaṃ, tūlikaṃ aḍḍhakāyikaṃ.

High couches; a snake; leg-supports, and legs of eight finger-breadths; thread, an eight-squared board, coarse cloth, a cotton-stuffed mattress, and a half-body pillow.

Giraggo bhisiyo cāpi, dussaṃ senāsanampi ca;

Onaddhaṃ heṭṭhā patati, uppāṭetvā haranti ca.

A mountain-top festival, and also bolsters; and cloth for the lodging; being bound underneath, it falls, and having torn it off, they steal it.

Bhattiñca hatthabhattiñca, anuññāsi tathāgato;

Titthiyā vihāre cāpi, thusaṃ saṇhañca mattikā.

The Tathāgata allowed decoration with various colors and decoration with the five fingers; in the monastery of the sectarians, and also in the monastery of monks, earth mixed with chaff and fine clay.

Ikkāsaṃ pāṇikaṃ kuṇḍaṃ, sāsapaṃ sitthatelakaṃ;

Ussanne paccuddharituṃ, pharusaṃ gaṇḍumattikaṃ.

Lac, 'monkey's hand' resin, earth mixed with broken rice, earth mixed with mustard powder, and beeswax oil; He allowed it to be removed when excessive; coarse earth, and earth from earthworm castings.

Ikkāsaṃ [T 2.0152] paṭibhānañca, nīcā cayo ca āruhaṃ;

Paripatanti āḷakā, aḍḍhakuṭṭaṃ tayo puna.

Lac, and the drawing of figures; a low parapet, and a climbing monk; they fall from the open verandah; a half-wall, and again, three cells.

Khuddake [M 0.0334] kuṭṭapādo ca, ovassati saraṃ khilaṃ;

Cīvaravaṃsaṃ rajjuñca, āḷindaṃ kiṭikena ca.

In a small monastery, the foot of the wall gets wet from rain; a loud sound, a wall-post; a bamboo robe-rail and a robe-rope, a terrace, and a window.

Ālambanaṃ [V 0.0313] tiṇacuṇṇaṃ, heṭṭhāmagge nayaṃ kare;

Ajjhokāse otappati, sālaṃ heṭṭhā ca bhājanaṃ.

A support, grass powder; one should follow the method in the way mentioned below. In an open space, it is heated by the sun; a stand for water pots, and a vessel below.

Vihāro koṭṭhako ceva, pariveṇaggisālakaṃ;

Ārāme ca puna koṭṭhe, heṭṭhaññeva nayaṃ kare.

A monastery, and a gatehouse; a surrounding compound, a fire-hall; and again in the monastery grounds and in the gatehouse, one should follow the very same method as below.

Sudhaṃ anāthapiṇḍi ca, saddho sītavanaṃ agā;

Diṭṭhadhammo nimantesi, saha saṅghena nāyakaṃ.

A plastered building. The faithful Anāthapiṇḍika went to the Sītavana; having seen the Dhamma, he invited the Leader together with the Saṅgha.

Āṇāpesantarāmagge, ārāmaṃ kārayī gaṇo;

Vesāliyaṃ navakammaṃ, purato ca pariggahi.

He gave orders on the way; a group of people had a monastery built. In Vesālī, new construction, and he had accepted it previously.

Ko arahati bhattagge, tittirañca avandiyā;

Pariggahitantaragharā, tūlo sāvatthi osari.

Who is worthy in the refectory? The partridge, and one not to be venerated; he accepted inside the village; a cotton mattress; he arrived in Sāvatthī.

Patiṭṭhāpesi ārāmaṃ, bhattagge ca kolāhalaṃ;

Gilānā varaseyyā ca, lesā sattarasā tahiṃ.

He had the monastery established, and there was an uproar in the refectory; the sick, and an excellent lodging; by a pretext, the group of seventeen monks were there.

Kena nu kho kathaṃ nu kho, vihāraggena bhājayi;

Pariveṇaṃ [T 2.0153] anubhāgañca, akāmā bhāgaṃ no dade.

By whom, indeed? How, indeed, did he divide by the monastery's share? The surrounding compound and the subsequent share; being unwilling, one should not give a share.

Nissīmaṃ sabbakālañca, gāhā senāsane tayo;

Upanando ca vaṇṇesi, ṭhitakā samakāsanā.

Outside the boundary, and at all times; there are three ways of receiving a lodging. Upananda praised those standing and those with an equal space.

Samānāsanikā bhindiṃsu, tivaggā ca duvaggikaṃ;

Asamānāsanikā dīghaṃ, sāḷindaṃ paribhuñjituṃ.

Monks with the same seat broke it; a group of three and a group of two. Monks with different seats; a long seat; using a mansion with a verandah.

Ayyikā ca avidūre, bhājitañca kīṭāgire;

Āḷavī [P 2.0179] piṇḍakakuṭṭehi, dvāraaggaḷavaṭṭikā.

An old woman not far away; it was divided in Kīṭāgiri. A monk from Āḷavī, plastering with patches and smearing walls; placing a door and a bolt-post.

Ālokasetakāḷañca[V 0.0314], geruchādanabandhanā;

Bhaṇḍikhaṇḍaparibhaṇḍaṃ, vīsa tiṃsā ca kālikā.

Smearing a window white and black; smoothing with red ochre, roofing, and binding. Placing a small shelf, repairing what is broken, and smoothing with cow-dung wash. For twenty years, for thirty years, and giving until the time the smoke ceases.

Osite akataṃ vippaṃ, khudde chappañcavassikaṃ;

Aḍḍhayoge ca sattaṭṭha, mahalle dasa dvādasa.

When finished, what is not done, what is unfinished. In a small monastery, for six and five years; in a monastery with a lean-to roof, for seven and eight years; in a large monastery, for ten and twelve years.

Sabbaṃ vihāraṃ ekassa, aññaṃ vāsenti saṅghikaṃ;

Nissīmaṃ sabbakālañca, pakkami vibbhamanti ca.

The entire monastery for one monk; they cause another to dwell in a Saṅgha monastery. Without a boundary and at all times; he has departed, and they disrobe.

Kālañca [M 0.0335] sāmaṇerañca, sikkhāpaccakkhaantimaṃ;

Ummattakhittacittā ca, vedanāpattidassanā.

He dies; a novice; a monk who has given up the training and one who has committed a terminal offense. An insane monk and one with a distracted mind; a monk afflicted by feeling and one who does not see the offense.

Appaṭikammadiṭṭhiyā, paṇḍakā theyyatitthiyā;

Tiracchānamātupitu, arahantā ca dūsakā.

A monk who does not remedy an offense and does not abandon a wrong view; a paṇḍaka; a thief-convert and a sectarian-convert. An animal; a matricide; a patricide; a killer of an Arahant; and a defiler of a bhikkhunī.

Bhedakā lohituppādā, ubhato cāpi byañjanakā;

Mā saṅghassa parihāyi, kammaṃ aññassa dātave.

A creator of schism, one who causes blood to flow, and one of both sexes. 'May the Saṅgha not decline'; the formal act is to be given to another.

Vippakate ca aññassa, kate tasseva pakkame;

Vibbhamati [T 2.0154] kālaṅkato, sāmaṇero ca jāyati.

When it is unfinished, it should be given to another; when it is finished, it is for that very monk. He departs, he disrobes, he dies, or he becomes a novice.

Paccakkhāto ca sikkhāya, antimajjhāpannako yadi;

Saṅghova sāmiko hoti, ummattakhittavedanā.

If one has renounced the training or has committed a terminal offense, the Saṅgha itself is the owner. Also in the case of an insane monk, one with a distracted mind, or one afflicted by feeling.

Adassanāppaṭikamme, diṭṭhi tasseva hoti taṃ;

Paṇḍako theyyatitthī ca, tiracchānamātupettikaṃ.

In the case of not seeing an offense, not remedying it, or not abandoning a wrong view, that monastery belongs to that very monk. A paṇḍaka; a thief-convert and a sectarian-convert; an animal, a matricide, and a patricide.

Ghātako dūsako cāpi, bhedalohitabyañjanā;

Paṭijānāti yadi so, saṅghova hoti sāmiko.

A killer of an Arahant, a defiler of a bhikkhunī, a creator of schism, one who causes blood to flow, and one of both sexes: if that monk confesses, the Saṅgha itself is the owner.

Harantaññatra [V 0.0315] kukkuccaṃ, undriyati ca kambalaṃ;

Dussañca cammacakkalī, coḷakaṃ akkamanti ca.

They carry to another place; a scrupulous monk. The woolen blanket falls down. A cloth, a hide, a foot-wiper, and a rough cloth: they tread on them.

Allā upāhanāniṭṭhu, likhanti apassenti ca;

Apassenaṃ likhateva, dhotapaccattharena ca.

With wet feet; a monk wearing sandals; a monk who spits. They scratch; they lean on. With a leaning-board, he just scratches. A monk who has washed his feet; with a bedsheet.

Rājagahe na sakkonti, lāmakaṃ bhattuddesakaṃ;

Kathaṃ nu kho paññāpakaṃ, bhaṇḍāgārikasammuti.

In Rājagaha, they are not able. Inferior food; a monk who assigns meals. How indeed to get a seat spread? The appointment of a storekeeper.

Paṭiggāhabhājako cāpi, yāgu ca phalabhājako;

Khajjakabhājako ceva, appamattakavissajje.

A monk who receives and distributes robes; a distributor of gruel and a distributor of fruit; a distributor of hard food; and one who gives out minor requisites.

Sāṭiyaggāhāpako ceva, tatheva pattaggāhako;

Ārāmikasāmaṇera, pesakassa ca sammuti.

A monk who gets the rain-cloths accepted, and likewise one who gets the bowls accepted. The appointment of a monastery-attendant messenger and a novice messenger.

Sabbābhibhū lokavidū, hitacitto vināyako;

Leṇatthañca sukhatthañca, jhāyituñca vipassitunti.

The All-Conqueror, the Knower of the World, the Leader with a mind for welfare, has permitted them for the purpose of seclusion and for comfort, for meditating and for practicing insight.

Senāsanakkhandhakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Chapter on Lodgings is finished.

7. Saṅghabhedakakkhandhakaṃ

7. The Chapter on Schism in the Saṅgha

1. Paṭhamabhāṇavāro

1. The First Recitation Section

Chasakyapabbajjākathā

The Account of the Going Forth of the Six Sakyans

330. Tena [T 2.0155][P 2.0180][M 0.0336][V 0.0316] samayena buddho bhagavā anupiyāyaṃ viharati, anupiyaṃ nāma mallānaṃ nigamo. Tena kho pana samayena abhiññātā abhiññātā sakyakumārā bhagavantaṃ pabbajitaṃ anupabbajanti. Tena kho pana samayena mahānāmo ca sakko anuruddho ca sakko dvebhātikā honti. Anuruddho sakko sukhumālo hoti. Tassa tayo pāsādā honti – eko hemantiko, eko gimhiko, eko vassiko. So vassike pāsāde cattāro māse vassike pāsāde vassike cattāro māse (sī.) nippurisehi tūriyehi paricārayamāno paricāriyamāno (ka.) na heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ orohati. Atha kho mahānāmassa sakkassa etadahosi – “etarahi kho abhiññātā abhiññātā sakyakumārā bhagavantaṃ pabbajitaṃ anupabbajanti. Amhākañca pana kulā natthi koci agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ vā pabbajeyyaṃ, anuruddho vā”ti. Atha kho mahānāmo sakko yena anuruddho sakko tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā anuruddhaṃ sakkaṃ etadavoca – “etarahi, tāta anuruddha, abhiññātā abhiññātā sakyakumārā bhagavantaṃ pabbajitaṃ anupabbajanti. Amhākañca pana kulā natthi koci agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito. Tena [T 2.0156] hi tvaṃ vā pabbaja, ahaṃ vā pabbajissāmī”ti. “Ahaṃ kho sukhumālo, nāhaṃ sakkomi agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajituṃ. Tvaṃ pabbajāhī”ti. “Ehi kho te, tāta anuruddha, gharāvāsatthaṃ anusāsissāmi. Paṭhamaṃ khettaṃ kasāpetabbaṃ. Kasāpetvā vapāpetabbaṃ. Vapāpetvā udakaṃ abhinetabbaṃ. Udakaṃ abhinetvā udakaṃ ninnetabbaṃ. Udakaṃ ninnetvā niddhāpetabbaṃ. Niddhāpetvā niḍḍahetabbaṃ, niḍḍahetvā (sī.) lavāpetabbaṃ. Lavāpetvā ubbāhāpetabbaṃ. Ubbāhāpetvā puñjaṃ kārāpetabbaṃ. Puñjaṃ kārāpetvā maddāpetabbaṃ. Maddāpetvā palālāni uddharāpetabbāni. Palālāni uddharāpetvā [P 2.0181] bhusikā uddharāpetabbā. Bhusikaṃ uddharāpetvā opunāpetabbaṃ ophunāpetabbaṃ (syā. ka.), ophuṇāpetabbaṃ (yojanā). Opunāpetvā atiharāpetabbaṃ. Atiharāpetvā [M 0.0337][V 0.0317] āyatimpi vassaṃ evameva kātabbaṃ, āyatimpi vassaṃ evameva kātabba”nti. “Na kammā khīyanti? Na kammānaṃ anto paññāyati? Kadā kammā khīyissanti? Kadā kammānaṃ anto paññāyissati? Kadā mayaṃ appossukkā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitā samaṅgībhūtā paricāressāmā”ti? “Na hi, tāta anuruddha, kammā khīyanti. Na kammānaṃ anto paññāyati. Akhīṇeva kamme pitaro ca pitāmahā ca [T 2.0157] kālaṅkatā”ti. “Tena hi tvaññeva gharāvāsatthena upajānāhi. Ahaṃ agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti.

330. At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Anupiyā, a market town of the Mallas. Now at that time, very well-known Sakyan princes were going forth in imitation of the Blessed One who had gone forth. At that time, Mahānāma the Sakyan and Anuruddha the Sakyan were two brothers. Anuruddha the Sakyan was delicate. He had three mansions: one for the winter, one for the hot season, and one for the rainy season. In the rainy-season mansion, for four months he was entertained by musicians who were exclusively female, and he did not descend to the lower part of the mansion. Then this thought occurred to Mahānāma the Sakyan: “Now, very well-known Sakyan princes are going forth in imitation of the Blessed One who has gone forth. But from our family, no one has gone forth from the household life into the homeless life. What if I were to go forth, or Anuruddha?” Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached Anuruddha the Sakyan and said this: “Dear Anuruddha, now very well-known Sakyan princes are going forth in imitation of the Blessed One who has gone forth. But from our family, no one has gone forth from the household life into the homeless life. Therefore, either you go forth, or I shall go forth.” “I am delicate; I am not able to go forth from the household life into the homeless life. You go forth.” “Come, dear Anuruddha, I will instruct you in the duties of the household life. First, the field must be plowed. After plowing, it must be sown. After sowing, water must be brought in. After bringing in water, it must be drained. After draining it, the field must be weeded. After weeding, the crop must be reaped. After reaping, it must be transported. After transporting it, it must be made into a heap. After making it into a heap, it must be trodden. After treading, the straw must be removed. After removing the straw, the chaff must be removed. After removing the chaff, it must be winnowed. After winnowing, it must be stored away. After storing it away, the very same must be done in the coming year; the very same must be done in the coming year.” “Do these tasks not come to an end? Is an end to these tasks not perceived? When will these tasks come to an end? When will an end to these tasks be perceived? When will we, free from care, furnished and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, enjoy ourselves?” “Indeed, dear Anuruddha, these tasks do not come to an end. An end to these tasks is not perceived. While the tasks were still unfinished, our fathers and grandfathers passed away.” “In that case, you yourself should attend to the duties of the household life. I shall go forth from the household life into the homeless life.”

Atha kho anuruddho sakko yena mātā tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā mātaraṃ etadavoca – “icchāmahaṃ, amma, agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajituṃ. Anujānāhi maṃ agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajjāyā”ti. Evaṃ vutte anuruddhassa sakkassa mātā anuruddhaṃ sakkaṃ etadavoca – “tumhe kho me, tāta anuruddha, dve puttā piyā manāpā appaṭikūlā. Maraṇenapi vo akāmakā vinā bhavissāmi. Kiṃ panāhaṃ tumhe jīvante anujānissāmi agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajjāyā”ti? Dutiyampi kho…pe… tatiyampi kho anuruddho sakko mātaraṃ etadavoca – “icchāmahaṃ, amma, agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajituṃ. Anujānāhi maṃ agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajjāyā”ti imassa anantaraṃ kesuci potthakesu evampi pāṭho dissati –- “evaṃ vutte anuruddhassa sakkassa mātā evamāha ‘sace tāta anuruddha bhaddiyo sakyarājā sakyānaṃ rajjaṃ kāreti agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, evaṃ tvampi pabbajāhī’”ti. Tena kho pana samayena bhaddiyo sakyarājā sakyānaṃ rajjaṃ kāreti. So ca anuruddhassa sakkassa sahāyo hoti. Atha kho anuruddhassa sakkassa mātā – ‘ayaṃ kho bhaddiyo sakyarājā sakyānaṃ rajjaṃ kāreti; anuruddhassa sakkassa sahāyo; so na ussahati agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitu’nti – anuruddhaṃ sakkaṃ etadavoca – “sace, tāta anuruddha, bhaddiyo sakyarājā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, evaṃ tvampi pabbajāhī”ti. Atha kho anuruddho sakko yena [T 2.0158] bhaddiyo sakyarājā tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā bhaddiyaṃ sakyarājānaṃ etadavoca – “mama kho, samma, pabbajjā tava paṭibaddhā”ti. “Sace te, samma, pabbajjā mama paṭibaddhā vā appaṭibaddhā vā sā hotu, ahaṃ tayā; yathā sukhaṃ pabbajāhī”ti. “Ehi, samma, ubho agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajissāmā”ti. “Nāhaṃ, samma, sakkomi agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitunti[P 2.0182]. Yaṃ te sakkā aññaṃ mayā [M 0.0338] kātuṃ, kyāhaṃ tyāhaṃ (sī. syā.) karissāmi. Tvaṃ pabbajāhī”ti. “Mātā kho maṃ, samma, evamāha – ‘sace, tāta anuruddha, bhaddiyo sakyarājā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, evaṃ tvampi pabbajāhī’”ti. “Bhāsitā kho pana te, samma, esā vācā. Sace te, samma, pabbajjā mama paṭibaddhā vā, appaṭibaddhā vā sā hotu, ahaṃ tayā; yathā sukhaṃ pabbajāhī”ti. “Ehi, samma, ubho agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajissāmā”ti.

Then Anuruddha the Sakyan approached his mother and said: “Mother, I wish to go forth from the household life into homelessness. Permit me the going forth from the household life into homelessness.” When this was said, the mother of Anuruddha the Sakyan said to Anuruddha the Sakyan: “My dear Anuruddha, you two sons are dear and beloved to me, not disagreeable. Even by death, I would be separated from you unwillingly. How then could I, while you are living, permit you the going forth from the household life into homelessness?” For a second time… For a third time, Anuruddha the Sakyan said to his mother: “Mother, I wish to go forth from the household life into homelessness. Permit me the going forth from the household life into homelessness.” Now at that time, Bhaddiya the Sakyan king was ruling the kingdom of the Sakyans, and he was a friend of Anuruddha the Sakyan. Then the mother of Anuruddha the Sakyan thought: “This Bhaddiya the Sakyan king is ruling the kingdom of the Sakyans and is a friend of Anuruddha the Sakyan; he will not be able to go forth from the household life into homelessness,” and she said to Anuruddha the Sakyan: “My dear Anuruddha, if Bhaddiya the Sakyan king goes forth from the household life into homelessness, then you too may go forth.” Then Anuruddha the Sakyan approached Bhaddiya the Sakyan king and said: “Friend, my going forth is connected with you.” “Friend, whether your going forth is connected with me or unconnected, let that be so. Go forth as you please.” “Come, friend, let us both go forth from the household life into homelessness.” “Friend, I am not able to go forth from the household life into homelessness. Whatever other deed I can do for you, what shall I do? You go forth.” “Friend, my mother told me this: ‘My dear Anuruddha, if Bhaddiya the Sakyan king goes forth from the household life into homelessness, then you too may go forth.’ And friend, you yourself spoke these words: ‘Friend, whether your going forth is connected with me or unconnected, let that be so. Go forth as you please.’ Come, friend, let us both go forth from the household life into homelessness.”

Tena [V 0.0318] kho pana samayena manussā saccavādino honti, saccapaṭiññā. Atha kho bhaddiyo sakyarājā anuruddhaṃ sakkaṃ etadavoca – “āgamehi, samma, sattavassāni. Sattannaṃ vassānaṃ accayena ubho agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajissāmā”ti. “Aticiraṃ, samma, sattavassāni. Nāhaṃ sakkomi sattavassāni āgametu”nti. “Āgamehi, samma, chavassāni…pe… pañcavassāni… cattāri vassāni… tīṇi vassāni… dve vassāni… ekaṃ vassaṃ. Ekassa vassassa [T 2.0159] accayena ubho agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajissāmā”ti. “Aticiraṃ, samma, ekavassaṃ. Nāhaṃ sakkomi ekaṃ vassaṃ āgametu”nti. “Āgamehi, samma, sattamāse. Sattannaṃ māsānaṃ accayena ubhopi agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajissāmā”ti. “Aticiraṃ, samma, sattamāsā. Nāhaṃ sakkomi sattamāse āgametu”nti. “Āgamehi, samma, cha māse…pe… pañca māse… cattāro māse… tayo māse… dve māse… ekaṃ māsaṃ… aḍḍhamāsaṃ. Aḍḍhamāsassa accayena ubhopi agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajissāmā”ti. “Aticiraṃ, samma, aḍḍhamāso. Nāhaṃ sakkomi aḍḍhamāsaṃ āgametu”nti. “Āgamehi, samma, sattāhaṃ yāvāhaṃ putte ca bhātaro ca rajjaṃ niyyādemī”ti. “Na ciraṃ, samma, sattāho, āgamessāmī”ti.

At that time, people were truthful and kept their word. Then Bhaddiya the Sakyan king said to Anuruddha the Sakyan, “Friend, wait for seven years. After seven years have passed, we shall both go forth from the household life into homelessness.” “Friend, seven years is too long. I cannot wait for seven years.” “Friend, wait for six years… five years… four years… three years… two years… one year. After one year has passed, we shall both go forth from the household life into homelessness.” “Friend, one year is too long. I cannot wait for one year.” “Friend, wait for seven months. After seven months have passed, we shall both go forth from the household life into homelessness.” “Friend, seven months is too long. I cannot wait for seven months.” “Friend, wait for six months… five months… four months… three months… two months… one month… half a month. After half a month has passed, we shall both go forth from the household life into homelessness.” “Friend, half a month is too long. I cannot wait for half a month.” “Friend, wait for seven days until I hand over the kingdom to my sons and brothers.” “Friend, seven days is not long; I will wait.”

331. Atha kho bhaddiyo ca sakyarājā anuruddho ca ānando ca bhagu ca kimilo ca devadatto ca, upālikappakena sattamā, yathā pure caturaṅginiyā senāya uyyānabhūmiṃ niyyanti, evameva caturaṅginiyā senāya niyyiṃsu. Te dūraṃ gantvā senaṃ nivattāpetvā paravisayaṃ okkamitvā ābharaṇaṃ omuñcitvā uttarāsaṅgena bhaṇḍikaṃ bandhitvā upāliṃ kappakaṃ etadavocuṃ – “handa, bhaṇe upāli, nivattassu; alaṃ te ettakaṃ jīvikāyā”ti. Atha kho upālissa kappakassa nivattantassa etadahosi – “caṇḍā [T 2.0160] kho sākiyā; iminā kumārā nippātitāti ghātāpeyyumpi maṃ. Ime [M 0.0339] hi nāma sakyakumārā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajissanti. Kimaṅga kimaṅga (sī.) panāha”nti. Bhaṇḍikaṃ muñcitvā taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ rukkhe ālaggetvā ‘yo passati, dinnaṃyeva haratū’ti [P 2.0183] vatvā yena te sakyakumārā tenupasaṅkami. Addasāsuṃ kho te sakyakumārā upāliṃ kappakaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna upāliṃ kappakaṃ etadavocuṃ – “kissa, bhaṇe upāli, nivattesī”ti? “Idha me, ayyaputtā, nivattantassa etadahosi – ‘caṇḍā kho sākiyā; iminā kumārā nippātitāti ghātāpeyyumpi maṃ. Ime hi nāma sakyakumārā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajissanti. Kimaṅga panāha’nti. So kho ahaṃ, ayyaputtā, bhaṇḍikaṃ muñcitvā taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ rukkhe ālaggetvā ‘yo passati, dinnaññeva haratū’ti vatvā tatomhi paṭinivatto”ti. “Suṭṭhu, bhaṇe upāli, akāsi yampi na nivatto yaṃ nivatto (sī.), yaṃ pana nivatto (syā.). Caṇḍā kho sākiyā; iminā kumārā nippātitāti ghātāpeyyumpi ta”nti.

331. Then Bhaddiya the Sakyan king, Anuruddha, Ānanda, Bhagu, Kimila, and Devadatta, with Upāli the barber as the seventh, set out with a fourfold army, just as they had previously gone to the pleasure grounds. Having gone a distance, they dismissed the army, entered a foreign territory, took off their ornaments, tied their belongings into a bundle with their upper robes, and said to Upāli the barber: “Come, friend Upāli, turn back; this much is sufficient for your livelihood.” Then, as Upāli the barber was turning back, this occurred to him: “The Sakyans are fierce; they might have me killed, thinking, ‘The princes were made to go forth by this one.’ Indeed, these Sakyan princes are going forth from the household life into homelessness; what then of me?” He untied the bundle, hung those goods on a tree, saying, “Whoever sees this, let them take it as a gift,” and approached the Sakyan princes. The Sakyan princes saw Upāli the barber coming from afar. Seeing him, they said to Upāli the barber: “Why, friend Upāli, have you turned back?” “As I was turning back, young lords, this occurred to me: ‘The Sakyans are fierce; they might have me killed, thinking, “The princes were made to go forth by this one.” Indeed, these Sakyan princes are going forth from the household life into homelessness; what then of me?’ So, young lords, I untied the bundle, hung those goods on a tree, saying, ‘Whoever sees this, let them take it as a gift,’ and have turned back from there.” “You have done well, friend Upāli, in not returning. The Sakyans are fierce; they might have you killed, thinking, ‘The princes were made to go forth by this one.’”

Atha [V 0.0319] kho sakyakumārā upāliṃ kappakaṃ ādāya yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu, upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te sakyakumārā bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “mayaṃ, bhante, sākiyā nāma mānassino. Ayaṃ[T 2.0161], bhante, upāli kappako amhākaṃ dīgharattaṃ paricārako. Imaṃ bhagavā paṭhamaṃ pabbājetu. Imassa mayaṃ abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānaañjalikammasāmīcikammaṃ karissāma. Evaṃ amhākaṃ sākiyānaṃ sākiyamāno nimmānāyissatī”ti nimmādayissatīti (sī.), nimmāniyissatīti (syā.).

Then the Sakyan princes, taking Upāli the barber, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those Sakyan princes said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, we who are called Sakyans are proud. This, venerable sir, is Upāli the barber, who has been our attendant for a long time. Let the Blessed One ordain him first. We will then pay homage to him, rise for him, greet him with joined palms, and perform the proper duties towards him. Thus, the Sakyan pride of us Sakyans will be subdued.”

Atha kho bhagavā upāliṃ kappakaṃ paṭhamaṃ pabbājesi, pacchā te sakyakumāre. Atha kho āyasmā bhaddiyo teneva antaravassena tisso vijjā sacchākāsi. Āyasmā anuruddho dibbacakkhuṃ uppādesi. Āyasmā ānando sotāpattiphalaṃ sacchākāsi. Devadatto pothujjanikaṃ iddhiṃ abhinipphādesi.

Then the Blessed One first ordained Upāli the barber, and afterwards those Sakyan princes. Then, within that very rains-retreat, the Venerable Bhaddiya realized the three knowledges. The Venerable Anuruddha produced the divine eye. The Venerable Ānanda realized the fruit of stream-entry. Devadatta produced the supernormal power belonging to worldlings.

332. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā bhaddiyo araññagatopi rukkhamūlagatopi suññāgāragatopi abhikkhaṇaṃ udānaṃ udānesi – “aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha”nti. Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu, upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ [M 0.0340] nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “āyasmā, bhante, bhaddiyo araññagatopi rukkhamūlagatopi suññāgāragatopi abhikkhaṇaṃ udānaṃ udānesi – ‘aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha’nti. Nissaṃsayaṃ kho, bhante, āyasmā bhaddiyo anabhiratova brahmacariyaṃ carati. Taṃyeva vā purimaṃ rajjasukhaṃ samanussaranto araññagatopi rukkhamūlagatopi suññāgāragatopi abhikkhaṇaṃ udānaṃ udānesi [T 2.0162] – ‘aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha’”nti.

332. At that time, the Venerable Bhaddiya, whether in the forest, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty dwelling, repeatedly uttered this inspired utterance: “Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!” Then many monks approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those monks said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the Venerable Bhaddiya, whether in the forest, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty dwelling, repeatedly utters this inspired utterance: ‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!’ Surely, venerable sir, the Venerable Bhaddiya practices the holy life without delight. Or perhaps, it is while recollecting his former happiness of kingship that he repeatedly utters this inspired utterance: ‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!’”

Atha kho bhagavā aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesi – “ehi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, mama vacanena bhaddiyaṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantehi – ‘satthā taṃ, āvuso bhaddiya, āmantetī’”ti[P 2.0184]. “Evaṃ bhante”ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato paṭissutvā yenāyasmā bhaddiyo tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ bhaddiyaṃ etadavoca – “satthā taṃ, āvuso bhaddiya, āmantetī”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho āyasmā bhaddiyo tassa bhikkhuno paṭissutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho āyasmantaṃ bhaddiyaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhaddiya, araññagatopi rukkhamūlagatopi suññāgāragatopi abhikkhaṇaṃ udānaṃ udānesi – ‘aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha’”nti? “Evaṃ bhante”ti. “Kiṃ pana tvaṃ, bhaddiya, atthavasaṃ sampassamāno araññagatopi [V 0.0320] rukkhamūlagatopi suññāgāragatopi abhikkhaṇaṃ udānaṃ udānesi – ‘aho sukhaṃ aho sukha’”nti? “Pubbe me, bhante, rañño satopi antopi antepure rakkhā susaṃvihitā hoti, bahipi antepure rakkhā susaṃvihitā hoti, antopi nagare rakkhā susaṃvihitā hoti, bahipi nagare rakkhā susaṃvihitā hoti, antopi janapade rakkhā susaṃvihitā hoti, bahipi janapade rakkhā susaṃvihitā hoti. So kho ahaṃ, bhante, evaṃ [T 2.0163] rakkhitopi gopitopi santo bhīto ubbiggo ussaṅkī utrasto viharāmi. Etarahi kho pana ahaṃ eko, bhante, araññagatopi rukkhamūlagatopi suññāgāragatopi abhīto anubbiggo anussaṅkī anutrasto appossukko pannalomo paradattavutto migabhūtena cetasā viharāmīti. Imaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, atthavasaṃ sampassamāno araññagatopi rukkhamūlagatopi suññāgāragatopi abhikkhaṇaṃ udānaṃ udānemi – ‘aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha’”nti. Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

Then the Blessed One addressed a certain monk: “Come, monk, in my name call the monk Bhaddiya, saying: ‘The Teacher calls you, friend Bhaddiya.’” “Yes, venerable sir,” that monk replied to the Blessed One. Having assented, he approached the Venerable Bhaddiya and said to him: “The Teacher calls you, friend Bhaddiya.” “Yes, friend,” the Venerable Bhaddiya replied to that monk. Having assented, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. To the Venerable Bhaddiya sitting to one side, the Blessed One said: “Is it true, Bhaddiya, as is said, that when you have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, you repeatedly utter the inspired utterance: ‘Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “But what advantage do you see, Bhaddiya, that when you have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, you repeatedly utter the inspired utterance: ‘Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!’?” “Formerly, venerable sir, when I was a king, protection was well-arranged inside the inner palace, and protection was well-arranged outside the inner palace; protection was well-arranged inside the city, and protection was well-arranged outside the city; protection was well-arranged inside the country, and protection was well-arranged outside the country. Though I was thus protected and guarded, venerable sir, I lived in fear, agitated, apprehensive, and terrified. But now, venerable sir, having gone alone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, I live without fear, without agitation, without apprehension, without terror, untroubled, with pride cast down, living on what is given by others, with a mind that has become like a wild deer’s. Seeing this advantage, venerable sir, when I have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, I repeatedly utter the inspired utterance: ‘Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!’” Then the Blessed One, having understood the meaning of this, on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance:

udā. 20 “Yassantarato [M 0.0341] na santi kopā, iti bhavābhavatañca vītivatto;

Taṃ vigatabhayaṃ sukhiṃ asokaṃ, devā nānubhavanti dassanāyā”ti.

For whom there are no inner angers, who has transcended both becoming and non-becoming; that one, free from fear, happy, and sorrowless—even the gods cannot get a sight of him.

Devadattavatthu

The Story of Devadatta

333. Atha kho bhagavā anupiyāyaṃ yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā yena kosambī tena cārikaṃ pakkāmi. Anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena kosambī tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā kosambiyaṃ viharati ghositārāme. Atha kho devadattassa rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – “kaṃ nu kho ahaṃ pasādeyyaṃ, yasmiṃ me [T 2.0164] pasanne bahulābhasakkāro uppajjeyyā”ti? Atha kho devadattassa etadahosi – “ayaṃ kho ajātasattu kumāro taruṇo ceva [P 2.0185] āyatiṃ bhaddo ca. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ ajātasattuṃ kumāraṃ pasādeyyaṃ. Tasmiṃ me pasanne bahulābhasakkāro uppajjissatī”ti.

333. Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Anupiyā as long as he pleased, set out on a journey toward Kosambī. Traveling by stages, he arrived at Kosambī. There the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī, in Ghosita’s Park. Then, while Devadatta was alone and in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind: “Whom, I wonder, should I win over, so that when he has faith in me, abundant gain and honor might arise?” Then this thought occurred to Devadatta: “This Prince Ajātasattu is young and has a prosperous future. What if I were to win over Prince Ajātasattu? When he has faith in me, abundant gain and honor will arise.”

Atha kho devadatto senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena rājagahaṃ tena pakkāmi. Anupubbena yena rājagahaṃ tadavasari. Atha kho devadatto sakavaṇṇaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā kumārakavaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā ahimekhalikāya ajātasattussa kumārassa ucchaṅge uccaṅke (syā.) pāturahosi. Atha kho ajātasattu kumāro bhīto ahosi, ubbiggo ussaṅkī utrasto. Atha kho devadatto ajātasattuṃ kumāraṃ etadavoca – “bhāyasi maṃ tvaṃ kumārā”ti? “Āma, bhāyāmi. Kosi tva”nti? “Ahaṃ devadatto”ti. “Sace kho tvaṃ, bhante, ayyo devadatto, iṅgha [V 0.0321] sakeneva vaṇṇena pātubhavassū”ti. Atha kho devadatto kumārakavaṇṇaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā saṅghāṭipattacīvaradharo ajātasattussa kumārassa purato aṭṭhāsi. Atha kho ajātasattu kumāro devadattassa iminā iddhipāṭihāriyena abhippasanno pañcahi rathasatehi sāyaṃ pātaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati, pañca ca thālipākasatāni bhattābhihāro abhiharīyati. Atha kho devadattassa lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūtassa pariyādinnacittassa evarūpaṃ icchāgataṃ [M 0.0342] uppajji – “ahaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pariharissāmī”ti[T 2.0165]. Saha cittuppādāva devadatto tassā iddhiyā parihāyi.

Then Devadatta, having put his lodging in order and taken his bowl and robes, set out for Rājagaha. Traveling by stages, he arrived at Rājagaha. Then Devadatta, concealing his own form, created the form of a young boy wearing a girdle of snakes and appeared on the lap of Prince Ajātasattu. Then Prince Ajātasattu was frightened, agitated, apprehensive, and terrified. Then Devadatta said to Prince Ajātasattu: “Are you afraid of me, Prince?” “Yes, I am afraid. Who are you?” “I am Devadatta.” “If you, venerable sir, are indeed the noble Devadatta, then please appear in your own form.” Then Devadatta, concealing the boy’s form, stood before Prince Ajātasattu wearing his three robes and carrying his bowl. Then Prince Ajātasattu, being deeply impressed by this miracle of psychic power performed by Devadatta, attended upon him morning and evening with five hundred chariots, and five hundred portions of food from cooking pots were brought as an offering of sustenance. Then to Devadatta, who was overcome by gain, honor, and fame, his mind seized by them, this evil desire arose: “I will lead the community of monks.” As soon as that thought arose, Devadatta fell away from that psychic power.

a. ni. 5.100 Tena kho pana samayena kakudho nāma koḷiyaputto, āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa upaṭṭhāko, adhunā kālaṅkato aññataraṃ manomayaṃ kāyaṃ upapanno. Tassa evarūpo attabhāvappaṭilābho hoti – seyyathāpi nāma dve vā tīṇi vā māgadhakāni māgadhikāni (syā.) gāmakkhettāni. So tena attabhāvappaṭilābhena neva attānaṃ na paraṃ byābādheti. Atha kho kakudho devaputto yenāyasmā mahāmoggallāno tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito kho kakudho devaputto āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ etadavoca – “devadattassa, bhante, lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūtassa pariyādinnacittassa pariyādiṇṇacittassa (ka.) evarūpaṃ icchāgataṃ uppajji – ‘ahaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pariharissāmī’ti. Saha cittuppādāva bhante, devadatto tassā iddhiyā parihīno”ti. Idamavoca kakudho devaputto. Idaṃ vatvā āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tattheva antaradhāyi.

At that time, a Koliyan prince named Kakudha, an attendant of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, had recently passed away and been reborn in a certain mind-made body. The body he acquired was of a size comparable to two or three Magadhan village-fields. With that acquired body, he harmed neither himself nor others. Then the deva Kakudha approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the deva Kakudha said to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: 'Venerable sir, for Devadatta, who was overwhelmed by gain, honor, and fame, his mind completely consumed, an evil wish of this sort arose: “I will lead the community of monks.” Venerable sir, as soon as that thought arose, Devadatta declined from that psychic power.' This is what the deva Kakudha said. Having said this, he paid homage to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, circumambulated him respectfully, and vanished right there.

Atha kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami[P 2.0186], upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi[T 2.0166]. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “kakudho nāma, bhante, koḷiyaputto mama upaṭṭhāko adhunā kālaṅkato aññataraṃ manomayaṃ kāyaṃ upapanno. Tassa evarūpo attabhāvappaṭilābho – seyyathāpi nāma dve vā tīṇi vā māgadhakāni gāmakkhettāni. So tena attabhāvappaṭilābhena neva attānaṃ na paraṃ byābādheti. Atha kho, bhante, kakudho devaputto yenāhaṃ tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā maṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito kho, bhante, kakudho devaputto maṃ etadavoca – ‘devadattassa, bhante, lābhasakkārasilokena abhibhūtassa pariyādinnacittassa evarūpaṃ icchāgataṃ uppajji – ahaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pariharissāmīti. Saha cittuppādāva bhante, devadatto tassā iddhiyā parihīno’ti. Idamavoca, bhante, kakudho devaputto. Idaṃ vatvā maṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tattheva antaradhāyī”ti.

Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, my attendant, a Koliyan prince named Kakudha, has recently passed away and been reborn in a certain mind-made body. The body he acquired is of a size comparable to two or three Magadhan village-fields. With that acquired body, he harms neither himself nor others. Then, Venerable Sir, the deva Kakudha approached me, paid homage to me, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Venerable Sir, the deva Kakudha said this to me: “Venerable sir, for Devadatta, who was overwhelmed by gain, honor, and fame, his mind completely consumed, an evil wish of this sort arose: ‘I will lead the community of monks.’ Venerable sir, as soon as that thought arose, Devadatta declined from that psychic power.” This, Venerable Sir, is what the deva Kakudha said. Having said this, he paid homage to me, circumambulated me to the right, and vanished right there.'

“Kiṃ [M 0.0343][V 0.0322] pana te, moggallāna, kakudho devaputto cetasā ceto paricca vidito? Yaṃ kiñci kakudho devaputto bhāsati sabbaṃ taṃ tatheva hoti, no aññathā”ti? “Cetasā ceto paricca vidito ca me, bhante, kakudho devaputto. Yaṃ kiñci kakudho devaputto bhāsati sabbaṃ taṃ tatheva hoti, no aññathā”ti. “Rakkhassetaṃ, moggallāna, vācaṃ. Rakkhassetaṃ, moggallāna, vācaṃ. Idāni so moghapuriso attanāva attānaṃ pātukarissati.

'But, Moggallāna, is the deva Kakudha known to you, having encompassed his mind with your mind? Whatever the deva Kakudha says, does it all happen just so, and not otherwise?' 'Venerable Sir, the deva Kakudha is known to me, having encompassed his mind with my mind. Whatever the deva Kakudha says, it all happens just so, and not otherwise.' 'Guard this speech, Moggallāna. Guard this speech, Moggallāna. Now that worthless man will reveal himself by himself.'

Pañcasatthukathā

The Discourse on the Five Teachers

334. a. ni. 5.100 “Pañcime[T 2.0167], moggallāna, satthāro santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmiṃ. Katame pañca? “Idha, moggallāna, ekacco satthā aparisuddhasīlo samāno ‘parisuddhasīlomhī’ti paṭijānāti ‘parisuddhaṃ me sīlaṃ pariyodātaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭha’nti. Tamenaṃ sāvakā evaṃ jānanti – ‘ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ satthā aparisuddhasīlo samāno ‘parisuddhasīlomhī’ti paṭijānāti ‘parisuddhaṃ me sīlaṃ pariyodātaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭha’nti ca. Mayañceva kho pana gihīnaṃ āroceyyāma, nāssassa manāpaṃ. Yaṃ kho panassa amanāpaṃ, kathaṃ naṃ mayaṃ tena samudācareyyāma? Sammannati kho pana cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārena – yaṃ tumo karissati, tumova tena paññāyissatī’ti. Evarūpaṃ kho, moggallāna, satthāraṃ sāvakā sīlato rakkhanti; evarūpo ca pana satthā sāvakehi sīlato rakkhaṃ paccāsīsati paccāsiṃsati (sī. syā.).

334. Moggallāna, there are these five teachers existing, being found in the world. What five? Here, Moggallāna, a certain teacher, being of impure virtue, claims: ‘I am of pure virtue,’ and ‘My virtue is pure, bright, and unblemished.’ His disciples know him thus: ‘This venerable teacher, being of impure virtue, claims: “I am of pure virtue,” and “My virtue is pure, bright, and unblemished.” If we were to inform the householders, it would not be pleasing to him. And that which is unpleasing to him, how could we address him with that? He is revered with robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick—whatever that one will do, by that he himself will be known.’ Thus, Moggallāna, disciples protect such a teacher in regard to virtue; and such a teacher expects protection from his disciples in regard to virtue.

“Puna caparaṃ, moggallāna, idhekacco satthā aparisuddhājīvo samāno ‘parisuddhājīvomhī’ti paṭijānāti ‘parisuddho me ājīvo pariyodāto asaṃkiliṭṭho’ti ca. Tamenaṃ sāvakā evaṃ jānanti – ‘ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ satthā aparisuddhājīvo samāno ‘parisuddhājīvomhī’ti paṭijānāti ‘parisuddho me ājīvo pariyodāto asaṃkiliṭṭho’ti [P 2.0187] ca. Mayañceva kho pana gihīnaṃ āroceyyāma, nāssassa manāpaṃ. Yaṃ kho panassa amanāpaṃ, kathaṃ na mayaṃ tena samudācareyyāma? Sammannati [T 2.0168] kho pana cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārena – yaṃ tumo [M 0.0344] karissati, tumova tena paññāyissatī’ti. Evarūpaṃ kho, moggallāna, satthāraṃ sāvakā ājīvato rakkhanti; evarūpo ca pana satthā sāvakehi ājīvato rakkhaṃ paccāsīsati.

Furthermore, Moggallāna, here a certain teacher, being of impure livelihood, claims: ‘I am of pure livelihood,’ and ‘My livelihood is pure, bright, and unblemished.’ His disciples know him thus: ‘This venerable teacher, being of impure livelihood, claims: “I am of pure livelihood,” and “My livelihood is pure, bright, and unblemished.” If we were to inform the householders, it would not be pleasing to him. And that which is unpleasing to him, how could we address him with that? He is revered with robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick—whatever that one will do, by that he himself will be known.’ Thus, Moggallāna, disciples protect such a teacher in regard to livelihood; and such a teacher expects protection from his disciples in regard to livelihood.

“Puna caparaṃ, moggallāna, idhekacco satthā aparisuddhadhammadesano samāno ‘parisuddhadhammadesanomhī’ti paṭijānāti ‘parisuddhā me dhammadesanā pariyodātā asaṃkiliṭṭhā’ti ca[V 0.0323]. Tamenaṃ sāvakā evaṃ jānanti – ‘ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ satthā aparisuddhadhammadesano samāno ‘parisuddhadhammadesanomhī’ti paṭijānāti ‘parisuddhā me dhammadesanā pariyodātā asaṃkiliṭṭhā’ti ca. Mayañceva kho pana gihīnaṃ āroceyyāma, nāssassa manāpaṃ. Yaṃ kho panassa amanāpaṃ, kathaṃ naṃ mayaṃ tena samudācareyyāma? Sammannati kho pana cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārena – yaṃ tumo karissati, tumova tena paññāyissatī’ti. Evarūpaṃ kho, moggallāna, satthāraṃ sāvakā dhammadesanato rakkhanti; evarūpo ca pana satthā sāvakehi dhammadesanato rakkhaṃ paccāsīsati.

“Furthermore, Moggallāna, here a certain teacher, being of impure Dhamma-teaching, claims: ‘I am of pure Dhamma-teaching,’ and ‘My Dhamma-teaching is pure, brilliant, and unblemished.’ His disciples know him thus: ‘This venerable teacher, being of impure Dhamma-teaching, claims: “I am of pure Dhamma-teaching,” and “My Dhamma-teaching is pure, brilliant, and unblemished.” If we were to tell the householders, it would not be pleasing to him. And what is unpleasing to him, how could we address him with that? He is esteemed with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—whatever he does, he himself will be known by that.’ Thus, Moggallāna, disciples protect such a teacher with regard to Dhamma-teaching; and such a teacher expects protection from his disciples with regard to Dhamma-teaching.

“Puna caparaṃ, moggallāna, idhekacco satthā aparisuddhaveyyākaraṇo samāno ‘parisuddhaveyyākaraṇomhī’ti paṭijānāti ‘parisuddhaṃ me veyyākaraṇaṃ pariyodātaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭha’nti ca. Tamenaṃ sāvakā evaṃ jānanti – ‘ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ satthā aparisuddhaveyyākaraṇo samāno [T 2.0169] ‘parisuddhaveyyākaraṇomhī’ti paṭijānāti ‘parisuddhaṃ me veyyākaraṇaṃ pariyodātaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭha’nti ca. Mayañceva kho pana gihīnaṃ āroceyyāma, nāssassa manāpaṃ. Yaṃ kho panassa amanāpaṃ, kathaṃ naṃ mayaṃ tena samudācareyyāma? Sammannati kho pana cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārena – yaṃ tumo karissati, tumova tena paññāyissatī’ti. Evarūpaṃ kho, moggallāna, satthāraṃ sāvakā veyyākaraṇato rakkhanti; evarūpo ca pana satthā sāvakehi veyyākaraṇato rakkhaṃ paccāsīsati.

“Furthermore, Moggallāna, here a certain teacher, being of impure exposition, claims: ‘I am of pure exposition,’ and ‘My exposition is pure, brilliant, and unblemished.’ His disciples know him thus: ‘This venerable teacher, being of impure exposition, claims: “I am of pure exposition,” and “My exposition is pure, brilliant, and unblemished.” If we were to tell the householders, it would not be pleasing to him. And what is unpleasing to him, how could we address him with that? He is esteemed with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—whatever he does, he himself will be known by that.’ Thus, Moggallāna, disciples protect such a teacher with regard to exposition; and such a teacher expects protection from his disciples with regard to exposition.

“Puna caparaṃ, moggallāna, idhekacco satthā aparisuddhañāṇadassano samāno ‘parisuddhañāṇadassanomhī’ti paṭijānāti ‘parisuddhaṃ me ñāṇadassanaṃ pariyodātaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭha’nti ca. Tamenaṃ sāvakā evaṃ jānanti – ‘ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ satthā aparisuddhañāṇadassano samāno ‘parisuddhañāṇadassanomhī’ti [M 0.0345] paṭijānāti ‘parisuddhaṃ me ñāṇadassanaṃ pariyodātaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭha’nti ca. Mayañceva kho pana gihīnaṃ āroceyyāma, nāssassa manāpaṃ. Yaṃ kho panassa amanāpaṃ, kathaṃ naṃ mayaṃ tena samudācareyyāma? Sammannati kho pana cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārena – yaṃ tumo karissati, tumova tena paññāyissatī’ti. Evarūpaṃ kho, moggallāna, satthāraṃ sāvakā ñāṇadassanato rakkhanti; evarūpo ca pana satthā sāvakehi ñāṇadassanato rakkhaṃ paccāsīsatīti. Ime kho, moggallāna, pañca [T 2.0170] satthāro santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmiṃ.

“Furthermore, Moggallāna, here a certain teacher, being of impure knowledge and vision, claims: ‘I am of pure knowledge and vision,’ and ‘My knowledge and vision is pure, brilliant, and unblemished.’ His disciples know him thus: ‘This venerable teacher, being of impure knowledge and vision, claims: “I am of pure knowledge and vision,” and “My knowledge and vision is pure, brilliant, and unblemished.” If we were to tell the householders, it would not be pleasing to him. And as for what is unpleasing to him, how could we address him with that? He is esteemed with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—whatever he does, he himself will be known by that.’ Thus, Moggallāna, disciples protect such a teacher with regard to knowledge and vision; and such a teacher expects protection from his disciples with regard to knowledge and vision. These, Moggallāna, are the five teachers existing, found in the world.

“Ahaṃ kho pana, moggallāna, parisuddhasīlo samāno ‘parisuddhasīlomhī’ti paṭijānāmi [V 0.0324] ‘parisuddhaṃ me sīlaṃ pariyodātaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭha’nti ca. Na ca maṃ sāvakā sīlato rakkhanti; na cāhaṃ sāvakehi sīlato rakkhaṃ paccāsīsāmi. Parisuddhājīvo samāno…pe… parisuddhadhammadesano samāno…pe… parisuddhaveyyākaraṇo samāno…pe… parisuddhañāṇadassano samāno ‘parisuddhañāṇadassanomhī’ti paṭijānāmi ‘parisuddhaṃ me ñāṇadassanaṃ pariyodātaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭha’nti ca. Na ca maṃ sāvakā ñāṇadassanato rakkhanti; na cāhaṃ sāvakehi ñāṇadassanato rakkhaṃ paccāsīsāmī”ti.

“But I, Moggallāna, being of pure conduct, claim: ‘I am of pure conduct,’ and ‘My conduct is pure, brilliant, and unblemished.’ My disciples do not protect me with regard to conduct, nor do I expect protection from them with regard to conduct. Being of pure livelihood… being of pure Dhamma-teaching… being of pure exposition… being of pure knowledge and vision, I claim: ‘I am of pure knowledge and vision,’ and ‘My knowledge and vision is pure, brilliant, and unblemished.’ My disciples do not protect me with regard to knowledge and vision, nor do I expect protection from them with regard to knowledge and vision.”

335. Atha kho bhagavā kosambiyaṃ yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā yena rājagahaṃ tena cārikaṃ pakkāmi. Anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena rājagahaṃ tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu, upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “devadattassa, bhante, ajātasattu kumāro pañcahi rathasatehi sāyaṃ pātaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati; pañca ca thālipākasatāni bhattābhihāro abhiharīyatī”ti. “Mā, bhikkhave, devadattassa lābhasakkārasilokaṃ pihayittha. Yāvakīvañca, bhikkhave[T 2.0171], devadattassa ajātasattu kumāro pañcahi rathasatehi sāyaṃ pātaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ gamissati[P 2.0188], pañca ca thālipākasatāni bhattābhihāro abhiharīyissati, hāniyeva, bhikkhave, devadattassa pāṭikaṅkhā kusalesu dhammesu, no vuḍḍhi.

335. Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Kosambī as long as he pleased, set out on a journey toward Rājagaha. Traveling in stages, he arrived at Rājagaha. There the Blessed One stayed in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. Then many bhikkhus approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, Prince Ajātasattu attends on Devadatta in the evening and the morning with five hundred chariots, and five hundred pots of cooked rice are brought as his meal offering.” “Bhikkhus, do not envy Devadatta’s gain, honor, and fame. For as long, bhikkhus, as Prince Ajātasattu attends on Devadatta in the evening and the morning with five hundred chariots, and five hundred pots of cooked rice are brought as his meal offering, only decline in wholesome qualities is to be expected of Devadatta, not growth.”

“Seyyathāpi[M 0.0346], bhikkhave, caṇḍassa kukkurassa nāsāya pittaṃ bhindeyyuṃ, evañhi so, bhikkhave, kukkuro bhiyyosomattāya caṇḍataro assa, evameva kho, bhikkhave, yāvakīvañca devadattassa ajātasattu kumāro pañcahi rathasatehi sāyaṃ pātaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ gamissati, pañca ca thālipākasatāni bhattābhihāro abhiharīyissati, hāniyeva, bhikkhave, devadattassa pāṭikaṅkhā kusalesu dhammesu, no vuḍḍhi.

“Just as, bhikkhus, if they were to place bile on the nose of a fierce dog, that dog would thereby become even fiercer, so too, bhikkhus, for as long as Prince Ajātasattu attends on Devadatta in the evening and the morning with five hundred chariots, and five hundred pots of cooked rice are brought as his meal offering, only decline in wholesome qualities is to be expected of Devadatta, not growth.”

saṃ. ni. 2.184; a. ni. 4.68 “Attavadhāya, bhikkhave, devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi, parābhavāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi.

“Bhikkhus, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his own destruction; for his downfall, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, kadalī attavadhāya phalaṃ deti, parābhavāya phalaṃ deti, evameva kho, bhikkhave, attavadhāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi, parābhavāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi.

“Just as, bhikkhus, a banana plant bears fruit for its own destruction, bears fruit for its downfall; even so, bhikkhus, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his own destruction, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his downfall.

“Seyyathāpi[V 0.0325], bhikkhave, veḷu attavadhāya phalaṃ deti, parābhavāya phalaṃ deti, evameva kho, bhikkhave, attavadhāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi, parābhavāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi.

“Just as, bhikkhus, a bamboo bears fruit for its own destruction, bears fruit for its downfall; even so, bhikkhus, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his own destruction, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his downfall.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, naḷo attavadhāya phalaṃ deti, parābhavāya phalaṃ deti, evameva kho, bhikkhave, attavadhāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi, parābhavāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi[T 2.0172].

“Just as, bhikkhus, a reed bears fruit for its own destruction, bears fruit for its downfall; even so, bhikkhus, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his own destruction, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his downfall.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, assatarī attavadhāya gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti, parābhavāya gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti, evameva kho, bhikkhave, attavadhāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādi, parābhavāya devadattassa lābhasakkārasiloko udapādī”ti.

“Just as, bhikkhus, a she-mule conceives for her own destruction, conceives for her downfall; even so, bhikkhus, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his own destruction, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his downfall.”

saṃ. ni. 1.183, 1.2.184, netti. 90 “Phalaṃ ve kadaliṃ hanti, phalaṃ veḷuṃ phalaṃ naḷaṃ;

Sakkāro kāpurisaṃ hanti, gabbho assatariṃ yathā”ti.

“Indeed, fruit destroys the banana plant, fruit the bamboo, and fruit the reed; honor destroys a wicked person, just as the fetus destroys the she-mule.”

Paṭhamabhāṇavāro niṭṭhito.

The First Recitation Section is finished.

2. Dutiyabhāṇavāro

2. The Second Recitation Section

Pakāsanīyakammaṃ

The Act of Proclamation

336. Tena [M 0.0347] kho pana samayena bhagavā mahatiyā parisāya parivuto dhammaṃ desento nisinno hoti sarājikāya parisāya. Atha kho devadatto uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “jiṇṇo dāni, bhante, bhagavā vuḍḍho mahallako addhagato vayoanuppatto. Appossukko dāni, bhante, bhagavā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraṃ anuyutto viharatu, mamaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nissajjatu. Ahaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pariharissāmī”ti. “Alaṃ, devadatta, mā te rucci bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pariharitu”nti. Dutiyampi kho devadatto…pe… tatiyampi kho devadatto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “jiṇṇo dāni, bhante, bhagavā vuḍḍho mahallako addhagato vayoanuppatto. Appossukko dāni, bhante, bhagavā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraṃ anuyutto viharatu, mamaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nissajjatu. Ahaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pariharissāmī”ti. “Sāriputtamoggallānānampi [T 2.0173] kho ahaṃ, devadatta, bhikkhusaṅghaṃ na nissajjeyyaṃ[V 0.0326], kiṃ pana tuyhaṃ chavassa kheḷāsakassā”ti! Atha kho devadatto – sarājikāya [P 2.0189] maṃ bhagavā parisāya kheḷāsakavādena apasādeti, sāriputtamoggallāneva ukkaṃsatīti – kupito anattamano bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Ayañcarahi devadattassa bhagavati paṭhamo āghāto ahosi.

336. At that time, the Blessed One was seated in an assembly that included the king, surrounded by a great retinue, teaching the Dhamma. Then Devadatta rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his hands in salutation toward the Blessed One, said this to him: ‘Venerable sir, the Blessed One is now aged, elderly, old, has advanced in years, and has reached the final stage of life. Venerable sir, let the Blessed One now, being free from exertion, dwell devoted to a pleasant abiding in this present life. Hand over the community of bhikkhus to me. I will lead the community of bhikkhus.’ ‘Enough, Devadatta. Do not desire to lead the community of bhikkhus.’ For a second time… and for a third time, Devadatta said this to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable sir, the Blessed One is now aged, elderly, old, has advanced in years, and has reached the final stage of life. Venerable sir, let the Blessed One now, being free from exertion, dwell devoted to a pleasant abiding in this present life. Hand over the community of bhikkhus to me.
